claim: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a debilitating inflammatory demyelinating disorder affecting millions worldwide.
source: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a debilitating inflammatory demyelinating disorder affecting millions worldwide (Reich et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reich et al., 2018

claim: MS causes dynamic changes to myelin in the central nervous system, including focal inflammatory destruction of myelin and remyelination.
source: MS causes dynamic changes to myelin in the central nervous system, including the quintessential focal inflammatory destruction of myelin, as well as the phenomenon of remyelination that can follow the demyelination (Lubetzki et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2014; Chari, 2007; Lassmann et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: Demyelinated axons are susceptible to persistent damage and neurological dysfunction in MS.
source: Demyelinated axons are susceptible to persistent damage and neurological dysfunction in MS; therefore, remyelination is a crucial aspect of tissue repair, and as such represents an important therapeutic target (Kremer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kremer et al., 2019

claim: Remyelination is a crucial aspect of tissue repair in MS and represents an important therapeutic target.
source: Demyelinated axons are susceptible to persistent damage and neurological dysfunction in MS; therefore, remyelination is a crucial aspect of tissue repair, and as such represents an important therapeutic target (Kremer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kremer et al., 2019

claim: Most knowledge about remyelination in MS derives from postmortem studies using histochemistry and electron microscopy.
source: Most knowledge about remyelination in MS derives from postmortem studies using histochemistry and electron microscopy.
evidence: Statement of established practice in the field

claim: Investigating remyelination in vivo in real time is limited by imperfect discrimination on neuroimaging modalities such as MRI.
source: This is because investigating remyelination in vivo in real time is limited by imperfect discrimination on neuroimaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
evidence: Statement of current limitation in the field

claim: In human beings, collecting serial short-interval scans is challenging, making it difficult to detect and track the dynamic occurrence of remyelination.
source: Furthermore, in human beings, where collecting serial short-interval scans is challenging, it is difficult to detect and track the dynamic occurrence of remyelination.
evidence: Statement of practical limitation in human studies

claim: Toxin models in mice, including the lysolecithin and cuprizone models, display demyelination and remyelination.
source: However, while toxin models in mice, including the lysolecithin and cuprizone models, display demyelination and even remyelination, they do not recapitulate the recruitment of peripherally derived adaptive immune cells that occurs in MS, which can potentially confound the MRI signal (Kipp et al., 2012; Kipp et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kipp et al., 2012 and 2017

claim: Toxin models in mice do not recapitulate the recruitment of peripherally derived adaptive immune cells that occurs in MS.
source: However, while toxin models in mice, including the lysolecithin and cuprizone models, display demyelination and even remyelination, they do not recapitulate the recruitment of peripherally derived adaptive immune cells that occurs in MS, which can potentially confound the MRI signal (Kipp et al., 2012; Kipp et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kipp et al., 2012 and 2017

claim: Rodent EAE models are often neither focally nor profoundly demyelinating and mostly impair the spinal cord.
source: Conversely, rodent experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) models, though driven by an immune response, are often neither focally nor profoundly demyelinating and mostly impair the spinal cord.
evidence: Statement of characteristics of rodent EAE models

claim: There is no known rodent model that is characterized by multifocal inflammatory demyelination in the brain that resembles MS and is disseminated in both space and time.
source: There is no known rodent model that is characterized by multifocal inflammatory demyelination in the brain that resembles MS and is disseminated in both space and time.
evidence: Statement of limitation in rodent models

claim: EAE in the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) is a well-recognized translational model that serves as a bridge between rodent EAE and human MS.
source: However, EAE in the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) is a well-recognized translational model that serves as a bridge between the rodent EAE and human MS (Jagessar et al., 2016; Kap et al., 2010; Kap et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jagessar et al., 2016; Kap et al., 2010; Kap et al., 2016

claim: Marmoset EAE resembles MS white matter lesions both radiologically and pathologically.
source: Not only does EAE resemble MS white matter lesions (WML) both radiologically and pathologically (Sati et al., 2012; Maggi et al., 2017), but marmoset WML spontaneously remyelinate (Lee et al., 2019), as occurs in MS.
evidence: Supported by citations to Sati et al., 2012 and Maggi et al., 2017

claim: Marmoset white matter lesions spontaneously remyelinate, as occurs in MS.
source: Not only does EAE resemble MS white matter lesions (WML) both radiologically and pathologically (Sati et al., 2012; Maggi et al., 2017), but marmoset WML spontaneously remyelinate (Lee et al., 2019), as occurs in MS.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2019

claim: Certain signal changes in MRI, such as magnetization transfer ratio (MTR), correlate with demyelination and remyelination in MS lesions.
source: Prior studies demonstrated that certain signal changes in MRI, such as magnetization transfer ratio (MTR), correlate with demyelination and remyelination in MS lesions (Chen et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2013; Filippi et al., 2012; Absinta et al., 2016; Laule and Moore, 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: MRI signal changes correlating with demyelination and remyelination have been investigated in animal models, mainly in rodent cortex rather than white matter.
source: This has also been investigated in animal models, albeit mainly in rodent cortex (Yano et al., 2018; Schmierer et al., 2010) rather than white matter.
evidence: Supported by citations to Yano et al., 2018 and Schmierer et al., 2010

claim: Partial remyelination can occur and can be localized either to specific parts of the lesion or to the whole lesion.
source: It has also been demonstrated that partial remyelination can occur and can be localized either to specific parts of the lesion (most commonly the lesion edge) or to the whole lesion (Filippi et al., 2019; Patrikios et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Filippi et al., 2019 and Patrikios et al., 2006

claim: EAE was induced in six marmosets and the animals were followed by MRI at regular intervals until sacrifice due to clinical progression.
source: EAE was induced in six marmosets as described, and the animals followed by MRI at regular intervals until sacrifice due to clinical progression.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure performed in this study

claim: Early active lesions at histopathology typically remained hyperintense on PDw images until the terminal scan.
source: Those categorized as 'early active' at histopathology typically remained hyperintense on PDw images until the terminal scan and grew rapidly to several cubic millimeters, subsequently showing minimal lesion volume change over time (example in Figure 1A–B) and were enhancing on terminal T1w MRI with gadolinium contrast.
evidence: Supported by data from the study and reference to Figure 1A-B

claim: Early active lesions grew rapidly to several cubic millimeters, subsequently showing minimal lesion volume change over time.
source: Those categorized as 'early active' at histopathology typically remained hyperintense on PDw images until the terminal scan and grew rapidly to several cubic millimeters, subsequently showing minimal lesion volume change over time (example in Figure 1A–B) and were enhancing on terminal T1w MRI with gadolinium contrast.
evidence: Supported by data from the study and reference to Figure 1A-B

claim: Early active lesions were enhancing on terminal T1w MRI with gadolinium contrast.
source: Those categorized as 'early active' at histopathology typically remained hyperintense on PDw images until the terminal scan and grew rapidly to several cubic millimeters, subsequently showing minimal lesion volume change over time (example in Figure 1A–B) and were enhancing on terminal T1w MRI with gadolinium contrast.
evidence: Supported by data from the study and reference to Figure 1A-B

claim: Lesions classified as 'chronic, at least partially demyelinated' demonstrated areas of PDw hyperintensity that persisted until the terminal scan despite resolution of early gadolinium enhancement on T1w images.
source: Lesions classified as 'chronic, at least partially demyelinated,' demonstrated areas of PDw hyperintensity that persisted until the terminal scan despite resolution of early gadolinium enhancement on T1w images (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by data from the study and reference to Figure 2A-B

claim: Lesions classified as 'remyelinated' were initially hyperintense on PDw images, with subsequent return toward isointensity over time.
source: Lesions classified as 'remyelinated' were initially hyperintense on PDw images, with subsequent return toward isointensity over time (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by data from the study and reference to Figure 3A-B

claim: None of the lesions returning to isointensity on PDw images demonstrated gadolinium enhancement on T1w images at terminal MRI.
source: None of the lesions returning to isointensity on PDw images demonstrated gadolinium enhancement on T1w images at terminal MRI.
evidence: Observation from the study data

claim: 40 focal white matter lesions were detected in the 6 EAE marmosets using in vivo MRI only.
source: Using in vivo MRI only, 40 focal WML were detected in the 6 EAE marmosets (Table 1).
evidence: Quantitative result from the study, referenced in Table 1

claim: Interrater reliability for PDw MRI classification was 94%, with Cohen's kappa of 0.89.
source: Interrater reliability for PDw MRI classification was 94%, with Cohen's kappa of 0.89, and consensus was achieved across the raters for all lesions.
evidence: Statistical measure of reliability from the study

claim: Of the 40 lesions detected by MRI, 12 (30%) were classified as predicted early active, 10 (25%) as predicted chronic at least partially demyelinated, and 18 (45%) as predicted remyelinated.
source: Of the 40 lesions, 12 (30%) were classified as predicted early active, 10 (25%) as predicted chronic at least partially demyelinated, and 18 (45%) as predicted remyelinated.
evidence: Quantitative results from the study

claim: Four of the six animals demonstrated predicted remyelinated lesions (M#1–4), whereas the remaining two only had predicted acute demyelinating and chronic, at least partially demyelinated lesions (M#5–6).
source: Four of the six animals demonstrated predicted remyelinated lesions (M#1–4), whereas the remaining two only had predicted acute demyelinating and chronic, at least partially demyelinated lesions (M#5–6).
evidence: Observation from the study data

claim: 31 lesions were identified in the 5 animals with postmortem tissue based on histological classification criteria.
source: Based on the histological classification criteria, 31 lesions were identified in the 5 animals with postmortem tissue (M#1 was not included in the histological analysis).
evidence: Quantitative result from histological analysis

claim: Of the 31 lesions identified histologically, 12 (39%) were classified as early active, 10 (32%) as chronic at least partially demyelinated, and 9 (29%) as remyelinated.
source: Twelve of the 31 lesions (39%) were classified as early active, 10 (32%) as chronic at least partially demyelinated, and 9 (29%) as remyelinated (Table 2).
evidence: Quantitative results from histological analysis, referenced in Table 2

claim: All three animals with predicted remyelinated lesions on MRI (M#2–4) had remyelinated lesions on histology.
source: All three animals with predicted remyelinated lesions on MRI (M#2–4) had remyelinated lesions on histology.
evidence: Comparison of MRI and histology results from the study

claim: M#5 and M#6 only harbored early active and chronic, at least partially demyelinated lesions, consistent with MRI findings.
source: M#5 and M#6 only harbored early active and chronic, at least partially demyelinated lesions, consistent with MRI findings.
evidence: Comparison of MRI and histology results from the study

claim: Two lesions in M#2 and one in M#4 were identified as predicted remyelinated on MRI but chronic, at least partially demyelinated on histology.
source: Two lesions in M#2 and one in M#4 were identified as predicted remyelinated on MRI but chronic, at least partially demyelinated on histology.
evidence: Discordant findings between MRI and histology from the study

claim: Of the 31 focal white matter lesions identified on both in vivo PDw MRI and histology, classification was concordant for 27 lesions (87%).
source: Of the 31 focal WML identified on both in vivo PDw MRI and histology, classification was concordant for 27 WML (87%).
evidence: Statistical comparison of MRI and histology results from the study

claim: PDw MRI predicted 19 demyelinated lesions and 12 remyelinated lesions, whereas histology showed 22 demyelinated and 9 remyelinated lesions.
source: When lesions were grouped by myelination status only (i.e. early active or chronic, at least partially demyelinated vs. remyelinated), in vivo PDw MRI predicted 19 demyelinated lesions and 12 remyelinated lesions, whereas histology showed 22 demyelinated and 9 remyelinated lesions (Table 3).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of MRI and histology results, referenced in Table 3

claim: Relative to histology, PDw MRI prediction was 100% sensitive and 90% specific for remyelination.
source: Relative to histology, PDw MRI prediction was therefore 100% sensitive and 90% specific for remyelination.
evidence: Statistical analysis of MRI performance relative to histology from the study

claim: The sensitivity and specificity of MTR for predicting remyelination, relative to histology, were 82% and 79%, respectively.
source: The sensitivity and specificity for predicting remyelination, relative to histology, were 82% and 79%, respectively.
evidence: Statistical analysis of MTR performance relative to histology from the study

claim: Across the six animals scanned longitudinally, 82% of the lesions newly detected on PDw MRI presented T1w gadolinium enhancement.
source: Across the six animals scanned longitudinally, 82% of the lesions newly detected on PDw MRI presented T1w gadolinium enhancement.
evidence: Quantitative observation from the study data

claim: Enhancement was occasionally seen at the following timepoint (10–15 days after first detection).
source: Enhancement was occasionally seen at the following timepoint (10–15 days after first detection).
evidence: Observation from the study data

claim: No chronic, at least partially demyelinated or remyelinated white matter lesions presented gadolinium enhancement on the terminal scan.
source: No chronic, at least partially demyelinated or remyelinated WML presented gadolinium enhancement on the terminal scan.
evidence: Observation from the study data

claim: M#5–6 presented at least one early active enhancing lesion at their terminal scan.
source: M#5–6 presented at least one early active WML enhancing lesion at their terminal scan.
evidence: Observation from the study data

claim: Inflammation and demyelination were dominant in lesions younger than 10 weeks of age.
source: Based on longitudinal MRI imaging of EAE lesions and analysis of normalized PDw signal intensity, with comparison to histology, we found that inflammation and demyelination were dominant in lesions younger than 10 weeks of age, corroborating previous work (Lee et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Observation from the study data, corroborated by citations to Lee et al., 2019 and 2018

claim: In four representative lesions that remyelinated, PDw signal intensity stabilized near baseline between 4 and 9 weeks after initial lesion detection on MRI.
source: In four representative lesions that remyelinated, PDw signal intensity stabilized near baseline between 4 and 9 weeks after initial lesion detection on MRI (Figure 4).
evidence: Observation from the study data, referenced in Figure 4

claim: Lesions larger than 0.5 µL at peak, as measured on PDw MRI, did not return to isointensity and correspondingly remained at least partially demyelinated on histology.
source: Lesions larger than 0.5 µL at peak, as measured on PDw MRI, did not return to isointensity and correspondingly remained at least partially demyelinated on histology.
evidence: Observation from the study data comparing MRI and histology

claim: Most lesions smaller than 0.5 µL returned to isointensity and appeared remyelinated on histology.
source: On the other hand, most lesions smaller than 0.5 µL returned to isointensity and appeared remyelinated on histology.
evidence: Observation from the study data comparing MRI and histology

claim: Of the 12 early active lesions, 7 showed an increased number of ASPA-/Olig2+ cells in the lesion vicinity.
source: Of the 12 early active lesions, 7 showed an increased number of ASPA-/Olig2+ cells in the lesion vicinity (Figure 5).
evidence: Quantitative observation from histological analysis, referenced in Figure 5

claim: The pattern of increased ASPA-/Olig2+ cells was never observed in remyelinated lesions or NAWM.
source: This pattern, never observed in remyelinated lesions or NAWM, suggests a possible proliferative OPC response, which may indicate attempted repair or potentially an inflammatory role of OPC in this setting (Harrington et al., 2020).
evidence: Observation from the study data

claim: The pattern of increased ASPA-/Olig2+ cells suggests a possible proliferative OPC response, which may indicate attempted repair or potentially an inflammatory role of OPC.
source: This pattern, never observed in remyelinated lesions or NAWM, suggests a possible proliferative OPC response, which may indicate attempted repair or potentially an inflammatory role of OPC in this setting (Harrington et al., 2020).
evidence: Interpretation of data with citation to Harrington et al., 2020

claim: In the context of marmoset EAE, PDw appears to have higher sensitivity and specificity for remyelination status compared to MTR.
source: In this study, we compared PDw and MTR MRI, since MTR is widely used to assay remyelination in vivo in MS (Chen et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2013; Mallik et al., 2014), and found that in the context of marmoset EAE, PDw, in close connection with histopathology, appears to have higher sensitivity and specificity for remyelination status.
evidence: Comparison of PDw and MTR results from the study

claim: MTR may be low in remyelinated lesions compared to healthy white matter because of the presence of incomplete or morphologically altered myelin sheaths.
source: MTR may be low in remyelinated lesions compared to healthy white matter because of the presence of incomplete or morphologically altered myelin sheaths (Brown et al., 2014; Mallik et al., 2014).
evidence: Explanation supported by citations to Brown et al., 2014 and Mallik et al., 2014

claim: MTR suffers from signal-to-noise reduction due to its calculation as a voxel-wise division of signal intensity measures.
source: Unlike MTR, which suffers from signal-to-noise reduction due to its calculation as a voxel-wise division of signal intensity measures, PDw signal intensity is directly measured by the MRI system, and thus PDw may prove more reliable for simply discriminating the presence or absence of remyelination and for characterizing its time course.
evidence: Technical explanation of MTR limitations

claim: PDw signal intensity is directly measured by the MRI system, and thus PDw may prove more reliable for discriminating the presence or absence of remyelination and for characterizing its time course.
source: Unlike MTR, which suffers from signal-to-noise reduction due to its calculation as a voxel-wise division of signal intensity measures, PDw signal intensity is directly measured by the MRI system, and thus PDw may prove more reliable for simply discriminating the presence or absence of remyelination and for characterizing its time course.
evidence: Inference based on technical characteristics and study results

source: We found no differences by corticosteroid treatment status in prevalence or time course of remyelination on either MRI or histological quantification.

source: On serial PDw MRI, 10 of 21 lesions (48%) were predicted to be remyelinated in corticosteroid-treated marmosets, compared to 8 of 19 (42%) in untreated animals.

source: Based on histological analysis in animals with available tissue, 4 of 12 lesions (33%) in corticosteroid-treated marmosets were remyelinated, compared to 5 of 19 (27%) lesions in untreated marmosets.

claim: The point biserial correlation model analysis showed that steroid administration had no significant correlation with remyelination detected on MRI (p=0.8).
source: The point biserial correlation model analysis showed that steroid administration had no significant correlation with remyelination detected on MRI (p=0.8).

source: The average experimental duration also did not differ (40 weeks in treated and 43 weeks in untreated marmosets; p=0.85).

claim: Histological analyses did not reveal differences between treated and untreated lesions.
source: Histological analyses also did not reveal differences between treated and untreated lesions.

claim: Assessment of PLP staining demonstrated larger unstained areas in early active (58 ± 25%) and chronic, at least partially demyelinated (38 ± 25%) lesions compared to remyelinated lesions (4.5 ± 1.1%) or NAWM (2.6 ± 0.3%).
source: Assessment of proteolipid protein (PLP) staining in 31 lesions and 10 normal appearing white matter (NAWM) areas (1500 µm2 centered over the lesion core) demonstrated larger unstained areas in early active (58 ± 25%) and chronic, at least partially demyelinated (38 ± 25%) lesions compared to remyelinated lesions (4.5 ± 1.1%) or NAWM (2.6 ± 0.3%) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Quantitative histological analysis from the study, referenced in Figure 5A

claim: LFB assessment showed 63 ± 26% unstained area in early active lesions, 43 ± 26% in chronic, at least partially demyelinated lesions, 15 ± 25% in remyelinated lesions, and 3.0 ± 0.4% in NAWM.
source: LFB assessment showed similar results: 63 ± 26% unstained area in early active lesions, 43 ± 26% in chronic, at least partially demyelinated lesions, 15 ± 25% in remyelinated lesions, and 3.0 ± 0.4% in NAWM (Figure 5B).
evidence: Quantitative histological analysis from the study, referenced in Figure 5B

claim: A significantly smaller unstained PLP area was observed in NAWM compared to remyelinated lesions (two-sample t-test, p<0.001).
source: We observed a significantly smaller unstained PLP area in NAWM compared to remyelinated lesions (two-sample t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison from histological analysis

claim: There were no apparent differences between PLP and LFB staining in the different lesion categories and in NAWM (two-sample t-test).
source: There were no apparent differences between PLP and LFB staining in the different lesion categories and in NAWM (two-sample t-test).
evidence: Statistical comparison from histological analysis

claim: One lesion appeared remyelinated on PLP, with less than 6% of unstained area, but demyelinated on LFB (82% of unstained area).
source: Interestingly, one lesion appeared remyelinated on PLP, with less than 6% of unstained area, but demyelinated on LFB (82% of unstained area).
evidence: Observation from histological analysis

claim: More mature oligodendrocytes were found in remyelinated lesions and NAWM than early active or chronic, at least partially demyelinated lesions.
source: Quantitative assessment of ASPA+/Olig2+ (mature oligodendrocytes) and ASPA-/Olig2+ (oligodendrocyte precursor cell [OPC]) across the 31 lesions and 10 NAWM areas showed, as expected, more mature oligodendrocytes in remyelinated lesions and NAWM than early active or chronic, at least partially demyelinated lesions (Figure 5C).
evidence: Quantitative histological analysis from the study, referenced in Figure 5C

claim: Significantly more oligodendrocytes were observed in NAWM compared to remyelinated lesions (two-sample t-test, p<0.001).
source: Consistent with PLP observations, we observed significantly more oligodendrocytes in NAWM compared to remyelinated lesions (two-sample t-test, p<0.001).

claim: More OPC were found in early active demyelinating lesions than in remyelinated lesions or NAWM.
source: Interestingly, more OPC were found in early active demyelinating lesions than in remyelinated lesions or NAWM (Figure 5D).

claim: The time course of marmoset EAE lesion development and repair is relatively stereotyped.
